sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Known T1DM vs T2DM; baseline insulin regimen (basal/bolus, pump)
Home A1c, last glucose monitoring
SGLT2 inhibitor use: risk for euglycemic DKA (glucose may <200 mg/dL)
Recent illness, infection, surgery, trauma
Medication compliance: missed insulin doses, new meds (steroids, atypicals)
Alcohol use (ketoacidosis, reduced food intake)
Pregnancy status (higher risk for DKA)
Prior episodes of DKA/HHS, prior ICU admissions

sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: DKA: anion gap acidosis + hyperglycemia + ketonemia (usually T1DM or insulin-deficient T2DM, precipitated by infection/nonadherence); HHS: extreme hyperglycemia (>600) + hyperosmolality + AMS without significant ketosis (T2DM); both present with polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, vomiting
Volume status: skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, cap refill, tachycardia, hypotension
Kussmaul respirations (deep, rapid: compensatory for metabolic acidosis)
Fruity breath (acetone)
Abdominal tenderness (common in DKA: may mimic surgical abdomen)
Mentation: lethargy: obtundation: coma (HHSmore severe AMS than DKA)
Signs of precipitant: fever, focal infection, new murmur, focal neuro deficits

pairs.value: DKA, lactic acidosis, renal failure (uremia), toxic ingestion (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates): MUDPILES mnemonic
DKA, HHS, stress hyperglycemia, steroidinduced, newonset DM, pancreatitis
Starvation ketosis, alcoholic ketoacidosis: glucose is normal or low
SGLT2 inhibitor use, pregnancy, reduced oral intake, alcohol use, liver failure: check ketones & AG even with normal glucose

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Orders:** IV access x2, Foley (strict I&Os — q1h), continuous SpO2, telemetry (K+ monitoring), q1h glucose checks
-**Stat labs:** BMP (glucose, K+, bicarb, BUN/Cr), VBG or ABG, serum ketones (betahydroxybutyrate preferred), CBC, lactate, serum osmolality, urinalysis
Check K+ BEFORE starting insulin: if K+ <3.3, replete K+ FIRST (insulin drives K+ intracellularly: fatal hypokalemia)
Search for precipitant: infection (#1), insulin noncompliance, newonset DM, MI, stroke, pancreatitis, pregnancy, meds (steroids, SGLT2i)
DKA & HHSpresent concurrently: mixed presentations have higher mortality than either alone
**More:** Acetaminophen level (r/o coingestion), lipase, troponin if MI suspected, blood cultures if febrile, CXR, ECG
**DKA monitoring:** POC glucose & betahydroxybutyrate q1h. BMP & pH q2–4h. K+ q2h (q1h if abnormal). Strict I&Os
**HHS monitoring:** Serum osmolality q2–4h (target ↓ 3–8 mOsm/kg/h). POC glucose q1h. BMP q2–4h. Strict I&Os

pairs.value: NS 1 L in first hour. If shock: rapid boluses with attention to airway. Then 250–500 mL/hr based on volume status. Replace deficits over 24–48h. Switch to D5½NS when glucose <250 mg/dL

Start 1–2h after fluids. Regular insulin 0.1 units/kg/hr IV infusion. Target glucose reduction ~50 mg/dL/hr & bicarb ↑ ~3 mEq/L/hr. If not meeting goals: ↑ by 1 unit/hr. When glucose <250: ↓ to 0.05 units/kg/hr & add D5 to IVF. Minimum rate 1 unit/hr to allow acidosis resolution
SQ rapidacting insulin q1–2h may used in ED or stepdown (safer, more costeffective). No significant outcome difference vs IV insulin when combined with aggressive fluids
Check K+ before insulin. If K+ <3.3: hold insulin, replete K+ first. Add 20–40 mEq KCl/L to IVF if K+ <5.0. Target K+ 4.0–5.0. Monitor q2h (q1h if abnormal)
Continue home basal dose or start glargine 0.3 units/kg early alongside IV insulin: prevents rebound hyperglycemia & facilitates SQ transition
Not routinely suggested: studies show no difference in acidosis resolution or time to discharge. Consider only if pH <6.9 with ↓ cardiac function or severe hyperkalemia
Not routinely replaced. Consider if severe deficiency present
Clinical improvement + pH >7.3 + betahydroxybutyrate normalized + bicarb ≥18 + anion gap closed + glucose <200 mg/dL. Do NOT stop insulin based on glucose alone: gap must close
NS (0.9% NaCl) is principal fluid. Replace ~50% of estimated fluid loss within first 12h. Fluid replacement alone will ↓ glucose. Switch to 5% or 10% dextrose when glucose <252 mg/dL (14 mmol/L)

Withhold insulin until glucose is no longer falling with IV fluids alone (unless ketonaemia present). When starting: 0.05–0.1 units/kg/hr. ↑ by 1 unit/hr as needed. Early insulin before adequate fluids is harmful in HHS

Measure/calculate serum osmolality regularly. Target reduction 3–8 mOsm/kg/h: rapid correction risks central pontine myelinolysis. An initial ↑ in Na is expected & is NOT an indication for hypotonic fluids
10–15 mmol/L (180–270 mg/dL) in first 24h: avoid overcorrection
Higher mortality than DKA. Risk of MI, stroke, seizures, cerebral edema, central pontine myelinolysis, VTE, foot ulceration. Prevent VTE with prophylaxis. Involve diabetes specialist team early
Osmolality <300 mOsm/kg + hypovolemia corrected (UOP ≥0.5 mL/kg/h) + cognitive status returned to baseline + glucose <270 mg/dL
Give basal SQ insulin 2–4h BEFORE stopping IV insulin to prevent rebound hyperglycemia & recurrent ketoacidosis. Overlap IV + SQ for 30–60 min minimum
If wellcontrolled on home regimen: resume home doses. If new: 0.5–0.8 units/kg/day total, with half as basal (glargine/detemir) & half as prandial (lispro/aspart) with meals
Giving lowdose basal analog early during IV infusion prevents rebound hyperglycemia without ↑ hypoglycemia risk

drugs.name: Normal saline (0.9% NaCl)
drugs.dose: 1 L in first hour, then 250–500 mL/hr
drugs.contraindications: Heart failure (use caution)
drugs.notes: Cornerstone of DKA & HHS tx. For HHS: replace ~50% deficit in first 12h.

drugs.name: Regular insulin
drugs.contraindications: K+ <3.3 (replete K+ first)
drugs.notes: Start 1–2h after fluids. ↓ to 0.05 units/kg/hr when glucose <250. Min rate 1 unit/hr for acidosis resolution. For HHS: may start at 0.05 units/kg/hr.

drugs.name: KCl replacement
drugs.contraindications: K+ >5.0, anuria
drugs.notes: Start when K+ <5.0 & UOP confirmed. Target 4.0–5.0. Monitor q2h (q1h if abnormal).

drugs.name: D5W or D10W
drugs.dose: Add to IVF when glucose <250 (DKA) or <252 (HHS)
drugs.contraindications: Hyperglycemia without concurrent insulin; avoid if osmolarity goal requires isotonic fluid
drugs.notes: Prevents hypoglycemia while insulin continues for acidosis/ketosis resolution.

drugs.name: Insulin glargine (basal)
drugs.contraindications: Hypoglycemia, allergy to glargine; do not give IV
drugs.notes: Give early alongside IV insulin for faster resolution & easier SQ transition. Give 2–4h before stopping IV insulin.

drugs.name: Sodium bicarb
drugs.contraindications: pH >6.9 (not routine)
drugs.notes: Not routinely suggested: no benefit shown in studies. Consider only if pH <6.9 with ↓ cardiac function or severe hyperkalemia.

pairs.value: Glucose >250 mg/dL + pH <7.3 + bicarb <18 + anion gap >12 + positive serum/urine ketones. All criteria must be met. ~10% present as euglycemic DKA (glucose <200): associated with SGLT2i, reduced intake, pregnancy, alcohol, liver failure
Mild: pH 7.25–7.30, bicarb 15–18. Moderate: pH 7.00–7.24, bicarb 10–15. Severe: pH <7.00, bicarb <10
Glucose >600 mg/dL + serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg + minimal/absent ketones + pH >7.3. Fluid deficit 100–220 mL/kg. Higher mortality than DKA
Infection (MCC), new T1DM/T2DM, insulin noncompliance, MI, stroke, pregnancy, meds (steroids, SGLT2i, atypical antipsychotics)

items: Diabetes type & home regimen: insulin (type, dose, timing), sulfonylurea, meglitinide
Last meal, PO intake, recent illness, vomiting, diarrhea
Recent medication changes: new insulin dose, ↑ sulfonylurea, added potentiator (fluoroquinolone, TMPSMX)
EtOH use: inhibits gluconeogenesis; causes prolonged hypoglycemia
Renal function: CKD ↓ insulin & sulfonylurea clearance
Adrenal insufficiency, liver disease, sepsis, malignancy, bariatric surgery hx
Betablocker use: masks adrenergic sx (tremor, tachycardia) but NOT diaphoresis
Intentional OD or insulin misuse: consider if recurrent or unexplained

sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: Adrenergic symptoms (diaphoresis, tremor, tachycardia, anxiety) appear first; neuroglycopenic symptoms (AMS, focal deficits, seizure, coma) follow if untreated — always check glucose in any patient with altered mental status
Adrenergic signs: diaphoresis, tremor, tachycardia, pallor, anxiety
Neuroglycopenic signs: confusion, slurred speech, ataxia, seizure, focal deficits, coma
Vitals: tachycardia, hypo or hypertension; hypothermia in severe cases
Signs of underlying cause: jaundice (liver failure), Kussmaul breathing (DKA overshoot), Addisonian features (hyperpigmentation, ↓ BP)
Injection sites: lipohypertrophy, signs of surreptitious insulin use

pairs.value: Exogenous insulin (most common in DM pts), sulfonylurea, meglitinide: check Cpeptide & insulin level
Prolonged hypoglycemia (up to 72h) from long halflife: requires octreotide & extended monitoring
Inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis. May present hours after drinking. Glycogen stores depleted in malnourished pts.
↓ cortisol: impaired gluconeogenesis & glycogenolysis. Check random cortisol.
↑ glucose consumption, hepatic dysfunction, ↓ glycogen stores
↓ glycogen storage & gluconeogenesis capacity
Rare. Fasting hypoglycemia with inappropriately ↑ insulin & Cpeptide. 72h supervised fast is gold standard dx.
Fluoroquinolones, TMPSMX, pentamidine, quinine, BB (mask sx), ACEi (rare)

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** Point-of-care glucose (immediately), BMP, insulin level + C-peptide (if spontaneous hypoglycemia), sulfonylurea screen
-**Orders:** IV access, continuous SpO2, telemetry, q15-30 min glucose checks until >100 mg/dL x2
Mild (54–70, alert): 15–20 g PO carbs: recheck 15 min: repeat PRN (Rule of 15). Follow with complex carb snack if next meal >1h.
Moderate (40–54, symptomatic): D50 25 g IV or D10 250 mL IV if peripheral line. Recheck q15 min.
Severe (<40, AMS, seizure): D50 25 g IV push. If no IV: glucagon 1 mg IM. Recheck q15 min. Consider D10 infusion.
Sulfonylureainduced: Octreotide 50–100 mcg SQ/IV q6–12h: prevents rebound hypoglycemia. Monitor 24–72h (prolonged effect).
EtOH related: D50 + thiamine 100 mg IV BEFORE or WITH dextrose (prevent Wernicke). D10 infusion until eating.
After correction: identify & address root cause: adjust insulin dose, hold sulfonylurea, treat infection, r/o adrenal crisis
Recheck glucose q15–30 min during active treatment, then q1–2h until stable >100 for ≥2 consecutive checks
If recurrent despite treatment: start D10 infusion at 75–125 mL/h & investigate underlying cause
**Fingerstick glucose:** STAT, then q15 min during treatment, q1–2h once stable
**BMP:** K+, Cr, Na: check renal function & electrolytes
**LFTs:** If liver disease suspected as contributor
**Cortisol / ACTH:** Random cortisol if adrenal insufficiency suspected (draw before giving steroids)
**Cpeptide & insulin level:** If cause unclear: draw DURING hypoglycemic episode. ↑ insulin + ↑ Cpeptide = endogenous (insulinoma, sulfonylurea). ↑ insulin + ↓ Cpeptide = exogenous insulin.
**Sulfonylurea screen:** If medication induced hypoglycemia suspected & pt denies use
**EtOH level:** If alcohol related hypoglycemia suspected
**Telemetry:** For glucose <54 or symptomatic: arrhythmia risk

drugs.name: Dextrose 50% (D50)
drugs.contraindications: Extravasation causes tissue necrosis: make sure good IV
drugs.notes: Firstline for severe hypoglycemia. Raises glucose ~75–100 mg/dL. Transient effect: follow with D10 or PO if needed.

drugs.name: Dextrose 10% (D10)
drugs.dose: 250 mL IV over 15–30 min or infusion at 75–125 mL/h
drugs.contraindications: Hyperglycemia without insulin coverage; not for use in fluid-overloaded pts without monitoring
drugs.notes: Gentler on veins than D50. Preferred for maintenance infusion or peripheral IV only. Avoids rebound spikes.

drugs.name: Glucagon
drugs.contraindications: Ineffective if glycogen depleted (EtOH, starvation, adrenal insufficiency)
drugs.notes: When no IV access. Onset 10–15 min. May cause N/V. Nasal formulation also available (3 mg).

drugs.name: Octreotide
drugs.contraindications: Biliary disease (gallstone risk), caution in DM (alters insulin secretion)
drugs.notes: Sulfonylureainduced hypoglycemia: suppresses insulin secretion, prevents rebound. Give for 24–72h.

drugs.name: Thiamine
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity to thiamine; IV/IM administration can rarely cause anaphylaxis
drugs.notes: Give BEFORE or WITH dextrose in EtOH related or malnourished pts: prevents Wernicke encephalopathy.

drugs.name: Diazoxide
drugs.contraindications: CHF, fluid overload
drugs.notes: For refractory hypoglycemia (insulinoma, nesidioblastosis): inhibits insulin release. Rarely used acutely.

pairs.value: Glucose <70 mg/dL. Clinically significant: <54 mg/dL. Severe: requires help from another person.
1) Sx consistent with hypoglycemia, 2) Low measured glucose, 3) Resolution of sx after glucose correction
Loss of adrenergic warning sx from recurrent episodes: common in T1DM & tightly controlled T2DM. ↑ risk of severe events.
Somogyi effect: overcorrection or counterregulatory hormone surge causing ↑ glucose after treatment

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: **Known adrenal insufficiency**; prior adrenal crisis; usual glucocorticoid replacement dose
**Triggers:**Recent GI illness, flulike illness, fever, infection, trauma, childbirth, surgery, extreme heat/cold exposure, or major emotional/physical stress
Abrupt stop/dec dose of chronic steroids: prednisone ≥5 mg/day for 4 weeks or longer can suppress HPA axis
Look for nonoral steroid exposure: inhaled steroids, steroid creams, joint injections, or exogenous glucocorticoids
**Meds**: levothyroxine start, phenytoin, phenobarbital, rifampin, carbamazepine, St John's wort, ketoconazole, etomidate, fluconazole, checkpoint inhibitors
Hx of autoimmune disease or polyglandular syndrome: type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease, vitiligo, pernicious anemia

sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: Hypotension refractory to fluids + hyponatremia + hyperkalemia in a patient on chronic steroids, with known adrenal insufficiency, or under physiologic stress without dose increase — can be rapidly fatal; give hydrocortisone empirically
↓ BP, orthostasis, tachycardia, signs of volume depletion
AMS ranging from lethargy/confusion to obtundation
Fever may present & can reflect trigger or cytokine driven stress response
Diffuse abdominal tenderness or pain may mimic an acute abdomen
Hyperpigmentation suggests primary adrenal insufficiency
Look for associated autoimmune findings or endocrine disease

pairs.value: Septic, hypovolemic, cardiogenic, & obstructive shock can all overlap; refractory ↓ BP is major adrenal crisis clue
Thyroid storm, myxedema coma, DKA, HHS, pituitary disease
Gastroenteritis, bowel obstruction, appendicitis, diverticulitis, pancreatitis, or causes of acute abdomen
Checkpointinhibitor endocrinopathy, adrenal metastases, adrenal hemorrhage, steroid withdrawal, antiadrenal drugs

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Orders:** IV access, aggressive IV fluids (NS 1 L bolus), continuous SpO2, telemetry, Foley (strict I&Os), endocrinology consult
-**STAT labs:** BMP/CMP, CBC, glucose, cortisol, ACTH, lactate, VBG/ABG, BCxs if infectious trigger suspected
Suspect adrenal crisis in hypotension or shock with AMS, vomiting, abdominal pain, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, or hypoglycemia.
Place pt on a monitor, give oxygen as needed, and get 2 IV lines.
Check point-of-care glucose immediately and give IV dextrose if low.
Draw BMP, glucose, and if helpful cortisol, ACTH, and cultures without delaying treatment.
Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately.
Start isotonic fluids with a 1 L normal saline bolus, then recheck and repeat as needed.
Continue hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h or 200 mg/day as an infusion.
Treat hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and other critical abnormalities per standard protocol.
Identify and treat the trigger, with early antibiotics if infection is suspected.
Escalate persistent hypotension to vasopressors and ICU transfer.
**Typical abnormalities:** Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, ↓ Glucose, prerenal AKI, metabolic acidosis; hypercalcemia can also occur
**Endocrine testing:** If stable enough, draw cortisol & ACTH before steroids. ACTH stimulation testing can help later, but never delay acute therapy
**Or workup:** Urinalysis, CXR, cultures, ECG, troponin, thyroid testing, or abdominal imaging depending on trigger & differential

pairs.value: Gastrointestinal infection / illness is common precipitating event
Infection, trauma, surgery, pregnancy, childbirth, strenuous activity, severe emotional stress, or any major physiologic insult
Abrupt cessation of glucocorticoids, antiadrenal medications, checkpoint inhibitors, & drugs that increase cortisol metabolism
Known adrenal insufficiency, prior adrenal crisis, primary adrenal insufficiency, older adults, multiple comorbidities, autoimmune polyglandular disease, type 1 diabetes
Starting levothyroxine in an untreated adrenal insufficient pt can precipitate crisis by increasing metabolic demand & cortisol clearance

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone
drugs.dose: 100mg IV/IM bolus, then 200mg over 24h (commonly 50mg IV q6h)
drugs.contraindications: Active untreated systemic fungal infection (relative; do not delay in crisis)
drugs.notes: Tx of choice.Don't delay treatment for labs. At doses >50mg/day, mineralocorticoid replacement isunnecessary acutely.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.contraindications: Active untreated fungal/bacterial infection (relative); caution in DM (↑ glucose)
drugs.notes: Alternative if diagnostic cortisol testing is still needed. Least preferred emergency alternative. No mineralocorticoid activity.

drugs.name: Prednisolone
drugs.dose: 25mg IV bolus, then 25mg x2 more doses in first 24h, then 50mg daily
drugs.contraindications: Active untreated infection (relative); caution in DM
drugs.notes: Preferred alternative parenteral steroid if hydrocortisone is unavailable.

drugs.name: Methylprednisolone
drugs.contraindications: Active untreated infection (relative); caution in DM, GI bleed
drugs.notes: Alternative steroid option if hydrocortisone is unavailable.

drugs.name: nl. saline
drugs.contraindications: Volume overload, hyperchloremic acidosis (relative)
drugs.notes: Cornerstone of initial resuscitation for hypovolemia & ↓ BP.

drugs.name: Dextrose 50%
drugs.contraindications: Hyperglycemia without insulin coverage; extravasation risk
drugs.notes: Treat ↓ Glucose now; continue glucose monitoring afterward.

drugs.name: Fludrocortisone
drugs.contraindications: Severe hypertension, hypernatremia, volume overload
drugs.notes: Add after stabilization in primary adrenal insufficiency if needed. Not required acutely when high dose hydrocortisone is being used.

pairs.value: ↓ BP that remains unexplained or resistant to standard fluid & vasopressor support
Weakness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, back pain, anorexia, dizziness, fever, confusion, syncope
Can worsen from nonspecific symptoms to shock, metabolic encephalopathy, obtundation, & coma
Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, volume depletion, salt craving, hyperpigmentation, higher risk than secondary adrenal insufficiency
Low cortisol with low or inappropriately nl. ACTH; aldosterone ispreserved, so hyperkalemia may absent
Patients with known adrenal insufficiencydouble or triple ir oral glucocorticoid dose during acute illness for 2-3 days depending on severity
Patients have emergency injectable hydrocortisone (or dexamethasone), saline, & syringes available
Encourage medical alert bracelet / necklace & steroid card with emergency dosing instructions
In undifferentiated shock, adrenal crisis ismissed b/c presenting symptoms are nonspecific: major bedside clue is persistent ↓ BP despite usual resuscitation

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Known hyperthyroidism or Graves' disease
Recent discontinuation of antithyroid Meds (PTU, methimazole)
Recent iodine load: contrast dye, amiodarone
Recent surgery, anesthesia, trauma, or sepsis (precipitants)
Med list: levothyroxine dose, anticholinergics, adrenergic drugs
Hx. of prior thyroid storm or thyroidectomy

sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: Severe hyperthermia + tachycardia/atrial fibrillation + AMS (agitation, delirium, coma) + a precipitant (infection, surgery, iodine load) in a patient with hyperthyroidism; Burch-Wartofsky score ≥45 = storm
High fever (often >40°C / 104°F), profuse diaphoresis
Tachycardia (often >140), irregular rhythm (AFib common)
Lid lag, proptosis, goiter, thyroid bruit
Hyperreflexia, fine tremor, proximal muscle weakness
AMS: agitation: confusion: obtundation: coma
Signs of CHF: JVD, crackles, peripheral edema

pairs.value: MCC. TSI antibodies. Proptosis, diffuse goiter, pretibial myxedema.
Nodular thyroid disease. Usually elderly pts.
Subacute, postpartum, or drug induced (amiodarone, checkpoint inhibitors)
Thyroid hormone OD (intentional or accidental)
Fever, tachycardia, AMS. Check TFTs in any unexplained multiorgan dysfunction.
Clonus/hyperreflexia, agitation, hyperthermia. Check Med list for serotonergic agents.
Paroxysmal HTN, tachycardia, diaphoresis, headache. Plasma/urine metanephrines.

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Orders:** IV access, continuous SpO2, telemetry (AFib monitoring), continuous temperature monitoring, cooling blanket (if hyperpyrexic), endocrinology consult
-**Labs:** CBC, BMP (hypercalcemia common), Mg, LFTs (hepatic dysfunction), ABG/VBG, lactate
**Step 1: Block new hormone synsis**: PTU 600–1000 mg load PO/NG: 200–250 mg q4–6h
**Step 2: Block sympathetic effects**: propranolol 1–2 mg IV q15min (max 10 mg) OR esmolol gtt 50–100 mcg/kg/min
**Step 3: Block T4, then T3 conversion**: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q6–8h (also prevents adrenal crisis)
**Step 4: Block hormone release** (give ≥1h AFTER PTU): potassium iodide (SSKI) 5 drops PO/NG q6h
Consult endocrinology STAT
Continue PTU + betablocker + hydrocortisone + iodine regimen
Monitor HR, temp, mentation q1–2h: gauge tx response
Serial TFTs q12–24h initially
Transition PTU: methimazole 20 mg PO q6h once stable (less hepatotoxicity)
Taper hydrocortisone over 3–5 days as pt improves
Treat precipitant: antibiotics if sepsis, address Med noncompliance
Refractory: consult nephrology for plasmapheresis or cholestyramine 4g PO QID (binds thyroid hormone)
**Stat:** TSH, free T4, free T3 (TSH undetectable, elevated fT4/fT3)
**ECG:** AFib/flutter(common), sinus tachycardia, ventricular arrhythmias
**Imaging:** CXR (pulmonary edema, cardiomegaly). Head CT if AMS to exclude or causes.
**Or:** BCxs (r/o sepsis as precipitant), cortisol level

drugs.name: PTU
drugs.contraindications: Liver failure
drugs.notes: Preferred over methimazole in storm: also blocks peripheral T4, then T3 conversion. Check LFTs.

drugs.name: Propranolol
drugs.contraindications: Asthma, severe CHF, ↓ HR
drugs.notes: Controls tachycardia & adrenergic sx. Also blocks T4, then T3. PO: 60–80 mg q4–6h.

drugs.name: Esmolol
drugs.contraindications: Asthma, severe CHF
drugs.notes: Ultrashort acting. Preferred if concerned ~betablocker tolerance.

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone
drugs.contraindications: Active untreated systemic fungal infection (relative; do not delay in crisis)
drugs.notes: Blocks T4, then T3 conversion. Prevents relative adrenal insufficiency. Taper over days.

drugs.name: SSKI (Iodine)
drugs.contraindications: Iodine allergy
drugs.notes: Give ≥1h AFTER PTU: otherwise feeds new hormone synsis (WolffChaikoff effect).

drugs.name: Acetaminophen
drugs.contraindications: Liver failure
drugs.notes: For fever. Avoid aspirin: displaces T4 from TBG, worsening free T4 levels.

pairs.value: Lifethreatening exaggeration of thyrotoxicosis with multiorgan dysfunction. BurchWartofsky score ≥45.
Excess thyroid hormone from any cause: Graves', toxic nodule, thyroiditis, exogenous thyroid hormone
≥45 = thyroid storm, 25–44 = impending storm. Components: temp, HR, AFib, CHF, GI/hepatic, CNS effects
10–30% even with tx. Early recognition & multiagent therapy are critical

sections.title: The First 60 Seconds
items: Airway: airway patent? Look, listen; suction if secretions/blood; jaw thrust if obstructed; call for airway help early
-If Pt looks terrible, can't protect airway: call ICU + anesthesia, then get ready to intubate
Breathing: RR, SpO2(good pleth?), WOB, accessory muscle use, paradoxical breathing, speaking in full sentences?
Start O2 now: NRB 15 L/min if in distress
Rapid O2 escalation if NRB insufficient: HFNC (up to 60 L/min, FiO2 up to 100%) → NIPPV → intubation
Circulation: HR, BP, perfusion; ↓BP, then tension PTX, PE, or cardiogenic shock
Put on cardiac monitor
Check fingerstick glucose.

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Known hypothyroidism: check compliance with levothyroxine. Recent dose changes or discontinuation
Prior thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine ablation, h/o Hashimoto thyroiditis
Precipitants (most common = infection): infection/sepsis, cold exposure, med nonadherence, surgery/trauma, MI, stroke, GI bleed
meds that worsen: amiodarone, lithium, sedatives, opioids, anesthetics, BB, diuretics, checkpoint inhibitors, TKIs
Recent sedation, surgery, or anesthesia: common inpt trigger
Baseline mentation: decompensationpresents as hypoactive delirium, not true coma
Comorbidities: CAD (thyroid replacement can unmask ischemia), adrenal insufficiency, pituitary dz (central hypothyroidism)
Prior TSH/T4 values, last labs

sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: AMS + hypothermia + bradycardia + hypoventilation in severe hypothyroidism; precipitants include cold exposure, infection, or sedatives in a patient with untreated or undertreated hypothyroidism
Classic triad: AMS + hypothermia + precipitating event
AMS (~90%): confusion, lethargy, obtundation —hypoactive delirium, not true coma despite name
Hypothermia (~70-90%): may severe (<32°C). Absence of fever despite infection is classic: hypothyroidism masks sepsis
↓ HR (~70%): sinus brady, may refractory to atropine
↓ BP:refractory to fluids & vasopressors until thyroid hormone given
Hypoventilation: shallow respirations, ↑ PaCO2
Skin: dry, coarse, cool, nonpitting edema (myxedema), periorbital edema
Delayed DTRs (hungup reflexes): slow relaxation phase
Macroglossia, hoarse voice
Ileus (↓ bowel sounds, distension), urinary retention
Hair loss (lateral eyebrows), brittle nails

sections.title: Hypothermia & Rewarming
items: Passive rewarming ONLY: warm blankets, ↑ room temp, warm IV fluids
Do NOT use active external rewarming (forced air, heating blankets at high temp): causes peripheral vasodilation: ↓ SVR: cardiovascular collapse in already hypotensive pt
Core temp may severely low (<32°C / 89.6°F): standard rmometers may not register
Use esophageal or rectal probe for accurate core temp
Goal: gradual rewarming ~0.5°C/h
Absence of fever does NOT r/o infection: hypothyroidism blunts febrile response. Treat empirically if any suspicion

pairs.value: Hashimoto thyroiditis (autoimmune, most common), postthyroidectomy, postradioactive iodine, radiation to neck, drugs (amiodarone, lithium, checkpoint inhibitors, TKIs)
Pituitary adenoma, Sheehan syndrome, pituitary surgery/radiation, infiltrative dz, TBI. TSH unreliable: check free T4
Sepsis, adrenal crisis, hypothermia (primary exposure), ↓ Glucose, drug OD (opioids, sedatives), stroke, CO poisoning
Adrenal crisis (check cortisol), severe sepsis, betablocker/CCB OD, ↑K, complete heart block, PE
Adrenal insufficiency (Schmidt syndrome: autoimmune thyroid + adrenal), or autoimmune disease (vitiligo, pernicious anemia, T1DM), acquired von Willebrand syndrome

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** TSH, free T4, free T3, CBC, BMP (Na+, Cr, glucose), cortisol, ABG/VBG
-**Orders:** IV access, continuous SpO2, continuous temperature monitoring (warming blanket), telemetry, endocrinology consult, ICU transfer
Give stressdose steroids BEFORE or concurrent with thyroid hormone: hydrocortisone 50mg IV q6h (or 100mg IV q8h). Giving T4 without steroids can precipitate adrenal crisis
IV levothyroxine (T4): loading dose 200-400 mcg IV push (lower dose for elderly, low body weight, cardiac dz). then 1.2 mcg/kg/day IV or 100mcg/day IV
IV route only: GI absorption unreliable in decompensated state (ileus, edema)
Passive rewarming ONLY: warm blankets, warm room. Avoid active external rewarming (can cause vasodilation: cardiovascular collapse)
IVF cautiously: pts may volumedepleted, but hyponatremia is common (dilutional from ↑ ADH). Avoid hypotonic fluids
Serial TSH, free T4, T3 q1-2 days: TSH ↓ ~50%/wk, free T4 normalize within 4 days
Vitals improvement expected 24-48h. Mentation may take days to weeks to normalize
Identify & treat precipitant: infection is most common but may masked (no fever, no leukocytosis). Low threshold for broad spectrum abx
Aggressive bowel regimen: ↓ motility, ileus risk
Stress ulcer prophylaxis
Avoid sedatives, opioids: can worsen/trigger decompensation
Monitor for cardiac ischemia during thyroid replacement: esp in elderly/CAD pts. EKG changes, troponin
Transition IV T4: PO levothyroxine when GI function returns & pt improving
Taper hydrocortisone once adrenal insufficiency excluded (cortisol, ACTH stim test)
DVT prophylaxis: immobile pts
Endocrinology consult for all pts: long term thyroid management
**TSH:** Markedly ↑↑ in primary hypothyroidism. May be lowith nl. in central hypothyroidism: do NOT rely on TSH alone
**Free T4:** Very low or undetectable. Key diagnostic test
**Free T3:** Often low. Useful for monitoring T3 replacement therapy
**Cortisol (random):** Draw BEFORE giving steroids. r/o concomitant adrenal insufficiency. If low: supports giving stressdose steroids
**BMP:** Hyponatremia (~50%: dilutional from ↑ ADH). ↓ Glucose. ↑ Cr (↓ renal perfusion)
**CBC:** Anemia (often macrocytic). Infection may NOT cause leukocytosis in myxedema
**ABG/VBG:** Check even without apparent resp distress: hypoventilation/hypercapnia common. Respiratory acidosis
**CK:** Often ↑ (hypothyroid myopathy, Rhabdo)
**Lipid panel:** Markedly ↑ cholesterol/TG (chronic hypothyroidism)
**BCxs, UA, CXR:** r/o infection as precipitant: remember fever may absent
**EKG:** Sinus ↓ HR, low voltage, prolonged QT, ± pericardial effusion (low voltage + electrical alternans)
**Monitoring:** TSH, free T4, T3 q1-2 days. TSH ↓ ~50%/wk. Free T4 normalize within 4 days

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone
drugs.contraindications: None in this emergency setting
drugs.notes: Give BEFORE or concurrent with thyroid hormone. Can precipitate adrenal crisis if omitted. D/C once adrenal insufficiency r/o (nl. cortisol, ACTH stim test)

drugs.name: Levothyroxine (T4) IV
drugs.dose: Loading: 200-400 mcg IV push. Maintenance: 100 mcg/day IV (or 1.2 mcg/kg/day)
drugs.contraindications: Acute MI (relative: use lower dose 100-200mcg), severe CAD (risk of ischemia/arrhythmia)
drugs.notes: Lower loading dose (100-200mcg) in elderly, low body weight, cardiac dz. IV only: GI absorption unreliable. Improvement in vitals expected 24-48h

drugs.name: Liothyronine (T3) IV
drugs.dose: Loading: 5-20 mcg IV. Maintenance: 2.5-10 mcg IV q8h
drugs.contraindications: Acute MI, unstable angina (relative: ↑ myocardial O2 demand)
drugs.notes: save for critically ill (hemodynamic instability, vent dependence, no improvement with T4 alone). More rapid onset than T4. D/C after 48h or if T3 levels ↑. Higher arrhythmia risk

drugs.name: Thiamine
drugs.contraindications: None
drugs.notes: Empiric: malnourished/chronically ill pts at Wernicke risk. Give before or with dextrose

drugs.name: Desmopressin (DDAVP)
drugs.contraindications: Hyponatremia (will worsen)
drugs.notes: Consider if hemorrhage: acquired von Willebrand syndrome can occur in severe hypothyroidism

pairs.value: Extreme decompensated hypothyroidism with endorgan dysfunction. Endocrine emergency. 30-60% mortality even with tx. Most pts are NOT truly comatose (misnomer)
Thyroid gl& failure (Hashimoto, postthyroidectomy, postRAI). ↑↑ TSH, ↓↓ free T4
Pituitary/hypothalamic cause. TSH may lowith nl./mildly ↑ despite low free T4. Can coexist with adrenal insufficiency ( must give steroids first)
Infection (most common), cold exposure, med nonadherence, surgery, MI, CVA, sedatives, opioids, amiodarone, lithium
Hypothyroidism may coexist with adrenal insufficiency (esp central). Giving thyroid hormone ↑ cortisol clearance: can precipitate adrenal crisis if cortisol is already low
